title: About
text:
Biography
Salutations! Today, I am a Visiting Assistant Professor in Political Science at St. Olaf College. The primary focus of my research investigates the structure and function of ethnic identity, with a focus on the effects of public policy on race and ethnicity in the United States and South Asia. I also have a secondary area of research on the politics of public support for judiciaries, and the contexts under which such support can protect judicial institutions from would-be autocrats.
Prior to St. Olaf, I completed my doctorate at George Washington University, where I studied how formal, government definitions of racial and ethnic identity in the United States influence perceptions of group boundaries. My dissertation, Boundaries of Belonging: The Structure and Stability of Ethnic Identity, was directed by Henry Hale, with Eric Kramon and Janet I. Lewis. I earned my M.A. in International Peace & Conflict Resolution from American University, with a focus on negotiation and mediation. During this time, I also served as a campus dialogue facilitator, helping students, staff, and faculty have meaningful (and often difficult) conversations around issues of race and racism on our campus.
Before starting my graduate studies, I lived in Guilin, China for two years where I worked as a foreign teacher and deputy director of international staff at Guangxi Normal University. I also hold a B.A. in International Relations and Politics (double major) and a B.S. in Biochemistry, Cell, and Molecular Biology from Drake University.

title: Research
text:
Overview
As a comparativist studying the effects of public policy on ethnic identity and political behavior, I focus on a variety of countries and regions including South Asia, the states of the former Soviet Union, China, the United States, and Brazil. Combined with my undergraduate background in biochemistry and graduate training in research methodology, my research portfolio is an eclectic mix of judicial politics, ethnic politics, survey methods, and Bayesian data analysis.

title: Research
text:
Boundaries of Belonging

Book project · Under development

Boundaries of Belonging: The Structure and Stability of Ethnic Identity


The book asks how ethnic boundaries and support for ethnically-targeted policies shift in response to variation in the way potential beneficiaries are defined. It draws on two original experiments fielded in May 2024 under a Doctoral Dissertation Grant from the Rapoport Family Foundation: a survey experiment among 1,800 White, Black, and Latino self-identifying adults in the United States, and a conjoint experiment among 900 Latino self-identifying adults. I find that individuals are more likely to perceive affirmative action as promoting equality of opportunity when eligibility is framed in more ascriptive terms, or when respondents themselves employ more ascriptive definitions of ethnicity. The conjoint complicates the picture – the two groups do not behave identically, and the difference is not one a single summary measure of ethnic attachment would capture. That gap is the manuscript’s central puzzle. I am preparing the manuscript for a major university press by 2028.

title: Research
text:
High Courts and Court-Curbing

Second book project · In progress

With Brandon Bartels and Eric Kramon, I am building a global account of when public support protects high courts from the leaders who would curb them. The project rests on a Bayesian dynamic latent trait model, borrowing from Christopher Claassen’s work on democratic mood, that pools survey data across time and space in order to produce country-year estimates of public support for high courts in 145 countries from 1981 to 2024. Merged with V-Dem measures of court-curbing, the estimates show that elite attacks raise the likelihood of court-curbing, that public support significantly attenuates that link, and that the attenuation is strongest precisely where theories of judicial independence have long assumed it would be, which is to say in more open societies and during moments of salient threats. The pieces below are selections from the larger project.



R&R · Comparative Political Studies

Can Public Support Insulate High Courts from Court-Curbing? Testing a Comparative Theory with a New Global Dataset


With Brandon Bartels and Eric Kramon


The idea that public support protects judicial independence is central to numerous theories in judicial politics. Yet this claim has been subjected to limited, direct empirical scrutiny in global context. We argue that public accountability and civil society mobilization are mechanisms through which the public can protect the judiciary, and that these mechanisms should matter most when courts face salient court-curbing threats. When elite attacks on courts increase the likelihood of court-curbing, public support significantly attenuates that connection. Our results have implications for literatures on judicial independence, judicial decision-making, and democratic erosion.



R&R · Political Science Research and Methods

Public Support for the Judiciary around the World: A New Cross-National Measure, 1981–2024


With Brandon Bartels and Eric Kramon


Public support features prominently in theory related to judicial independence and judicial power. Yet a lack of globally comparable data, across countries and over time, has limited researchers’ ability to test these ideas. This paper introduces the first global measure of public support for the judiciary that addresses this gap. We produce country-year estimates by gathering courts-related measures of trust, satisfaction, and approval from international surveys and estimating a Bayesian group-level dynamic item-response-theory model, and we provide evidence of construct, convergent, discriminant, and predictive validity using independent V-Dem data. These data create new opportunities to study how the public shapes judicial independence, power, and the rule of law.

title: Research
text:
Peer-Reviewed Articles


The Dimensions of Ethnicity: Understanding the Cognitive Architecture of Ethnic Group Membership


Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics, 2026, 1–34 · doi:10.1017/rep.2026.10070


What makes someone belong to an ethnic group? This article examines how individuals organize and prioritize ethnic attributes frequently used to denote membership and asks when simplified measurement strategies provide a reasonable approximation of ethnic identity in practice. Using original survey data from two online experiments fielded in 2024, I analyze respondents’ evaluations of eight common identity attributes among White, Black, and Latino Americans. Drawing on principal components analysis, multidimensional preference scaling, and circular-linear regression, I show that while some identities are well approximated by a single dominant dimension, others exhibit weaker alignment and greater heterogeneity in how attributes are prioritized. These differences have direct implications for measurement: reliance on any single attribute can meaningfully capture some identities while systematically misrepresenting others. More broadly, the findings underscore the need for group-sensitive measurement strategies when studying ethnic identity and its political and social consequences.




The Myth of Ethnicity: Understanding the Relationship Between Genotype, Phenotype, and Ethnotype


Ethnopolitics, 2025, 1–24 · doi:10.1080/17449057.2025.2464506


The explosion of at-home DNA ancestry testing has unsettled how people understand their ethnic heritage and how they choose to identify. Behind these tests lies a critical intuition: if all ethnic identities have some combination of descent-based attributes in common, then they must have some combination of genetic material in common as well. But does genetic ancestry testing actually allow us to determine ethnicity? This article places the literature on ethnic identity into conversation with advances in genetic science and commercial genealogy to explain why the latter is incapable of predicting the former. The subjectivity inherent in selecting a system of categorization and the properties of gene expression and replication illustrate the difficulties involved in linking one concept to the other. Ultimately, this paper suggests that future technological advancements are unlikely to resolve these tensions, and urges the field of political science to be vigilant in educating communities about the differences between genetic ancestry and ethnotype.

text:
Planned Work

Prospective

A Tamil Nadu extension


I plan to adapt my measurement approach for self-identified Tamils and Vanniyars in India. Both identities are highly salient and Tamil Nadu maintains reservations for both, which makes the state an unusually direct test of whether the American findings travel. The study has not yet been fielded.



Prospective

A group-deliberation conjoint


A replication of the conjoint experiment that replaces individual respondents with small discussion groups, in order to test whether classification norms emerge from aggregated individual views or from interaction itself.

title: Teaching
text:
Philosophy
As an educator, I believe it is important to remember what it was like to be a student (and to be sensitive to how much things have changed!). While coursework is and should be the primary focus for undergraduate students, it is hardly the only demand on their time. Nor is it the only way for students to mature and grow during their time in school.
With this in mind, I design my courses with an eye towards engaging as many of our senses, experiences, and backgrounds as possible. Especially in the age of GAI, this helps not only to spur participation and maximize retention, but also to illustrate the relevance and applicability of the skills and knowledge we build together. If an instructor tells us something, we may or may not remember. And simply asking students to write ensures at least some will choose the path of least resistance. But if we are challenged to apply that knowledge, we have a chance to practice empathy and gain a deeper, more intuitive understanding of the types of decisions facing political actors each and every day.
Experiential Learning

title: Teaching
section: Two Ways of Doing the Same Thing
text:
Two Ways of Doing the Same Thing
Nearly everything I teach runs through one of two modes of experiential learning. In my substantive courses the format is simulation; in the research methods course it is the lab. From the doorway they look almost nothing alike, and a visitor who walked past a plenary session of the Congress of Vienna on Wednesday and a room full of students staring at regression output on Thursday would be forgiven for concluding that the two courses had been designed by different people, but they rest on the same conviction: that a student should have to operate a concept rather than restate it, and should be assessed on how they operates it rather than on whether they happened to come out ahead. A delegate is not graded on keeping they territory. A student conducting surveys is not graded on finding a significant coefficient. Both are graded on what they did with what they had, and on whether they can say afterward why they did it.

title: Teaching
text:
Simulations

A student can be told what it feels like to run out of time, out of allies, and out of good options. It tends to land rather differently when it happens to them on a Thursday afternoon.

Because so much of the work in these courses happens out loud and in front of other people, I have tried to build an assessment scheme that measures it where it actually occurs. Drawing on the Reacting to the Past pedagogy, students are graded on formal speeches delivered in class, on writing produced in role (e.g. position papers; treaties; edicts; the occasional furious petition), and on reflective writings in which they step outside their character in order to make sense of what they and their classmates actually did. I define participation in advance and in writing, rather than leaving it to whatever impression I happen to have formed by the end of the term. Students who are not naturally inclined to speak first deserve to know what is being asked of them and when it is coming.
Alongside the multi-week games, shorter simulations run throughout the semester: two-level bargaining, coalition formation, and crisis negotiation against a deadline. In my World Politics course, there are five of these before the Congress of Vienna begins, and they carry a quarter of the grade on their own, which is deliberate – a student who has never had to improvise under time pressure in a low-stakes room will not suddenly manage it in a plenary session with forty percent of the course riding on it. The aim throughout is that a concept introduced in Monday’s reading is something students have to attempt to implement themselves by Friday. Thus the reading is not a prelude to the work of the course; it is equipment for it.

title: Teaching
text:
Labs
Analyzing Politics covers case studies, ethnography, archival research, content analysis, surveys, experiments, statistical modeling, and how to use R, which is a great deal of ground for a single required sophomore course. Each method we discuss is paired with a guided lab in which students work through it themselves rather than watch me present it on a slide. I focus on helping students understand the intuitions behind the approach before the mechanics themselves, and the ordering is deliberate rather than incidental: a student who can execute code without knowing what the code is doing has learned something, but not the thing the course exists to teach. In the hypothesis testing portion of the course we run most of our work through a single question – is this result actually weird? – which carries students a good deal further than the formal vocabulary does, at least until they have enough intuition to hang the formal vocabulary on.
The labs themselves vary with the method. When we discuss ethnography, two thirds of the class become research subjects competing at some deliberately absurd task – building the tallest structure they can manage out of drinking straws, say – while the remaining third take on the role of budding ethnographers and record what they observe. When I teach archival work, students are handed a mini-archive on the Falcon Lake incident, a 1967 UFO sighting in Manitoba whose documentary record is fragmentary, mutually contradictory, and entirely earnest in tone, which is precisely what recommends it. Other sessions run interviews, or a survey experiment in which the students are themselves the respondents, so that the framing effects they will later encounter in published work are ones they have already been subjected to without noticing.
Labs are graded entirely on participation, in parallel to my approach to simulations: a student who conducts a clumsy interview and can explain afterward what went wrong has done the assignment, while a student who produces a clean transcript without noticing that she led her respondent has not. In this way the cost of attempting a method and failing at it is held at zero, which is the only condition under which a sophomore will attempt eight of them in a single semester.
The cumulative work sits elsewhere. Each student carries one research question from the first week of the term to the last, and the requirement is that they attempt to answer it twice, once with a qualitative method and once with a quantitative one. The aim is not that anyone should leave with a favorite. It is that they should leave having actually done political science in several of its modes, and knowing from the inside, rather than from a textbook’s summary of the methodological debate, what each of those modes can and cannot tell you about a question they have chosen and care about.

title: Caleb H. Schmotter
text:
Caleb H. Schmotter



Comparative Politics · Political Behavior

Caleb H. Schmotter


Visiting Assistant Professor of Political Science St. Olaf College





For fifteen years I have been putting students into rooms where they must argue as delegates, monarchs, and ministers, and where the outcome is genuinely in doubt. My research comprises two book projects: the first centers on the formation and evolution of ethnic boundaries, while the second tests the impact of public support on judicial independence.




Currently Teaching · Fall 2026


PSCI 220

Analyzing Politics


The required sophomore methods course, covering case studies, ethnography, archival research, content analysis, surveys, experiments, statistical modeling, and R. Students learn how to conduct research, present results, and understand “how we know what we know” in political science.



PSCI 258

World Politics


A sophomore course in international relations built around negotiation skills and analysis. Five in-class simulations lead into the capstone: a five-week reconstruction of the Congress of Vienna in which students take assigned diplomatic roles, write to their sovereigns, and argue the fate of post-Napoleonic Europe across plenary sessions and commissions. Throughout the semester, they also keep a journal of negotiations from their own lives with the goal of improving their ability to self-advocate while also reaching sustainable agreements.




In the Classroom

My first classroom was a Reacting to the Past seminar at Drake in 2010, where over three years I served as a teaching assistant for four games: Henry VIII and the Reformation Parliament; The Threshold of Democracy: Athens in 403 B.C.; Defining a Nation: India on the Eve of Independence, 1945; and Confucianism and the Succession Crisis of the Wanli Emperor, 1587. I taught the Athens game on my own at Guangxi Normal University in 2015, and I have since built original courses on the same model – Tyrants, Demagogues, and Democrats draws on the Athens and India games, and Maladroit Monarchs on the English and Ming ones. This fall I am running the Congress of Vienna for the first time, as the capstone of World Politics. The method asks students to take on historical figures and argue toward outcomes that remain genuinely uncertain, governed by primary texts, by the victory conditions each player is handed in private, and above all by the actions of other students, which no amount of preparation on my part can predict and which regularly deliver results that the historical record did not. If I simply tell a class that coalitions are fragile, they may or may not remember it; if a student spends three weeks assembling one and then watches it come apart in the session before the final vote, the lesson tends to stick. The difference is not subtle. In this way, fifteen years of this work have convinced me that the most durable thing a simulation teaches is not just its historical content but the procedural intuition underneath it.

The Dimensions of Ethnicity: Understanding the Cognitive Architecture of Ethnic Group Membership

The article rests on two original experiments fielded in May 2024 under a Rapoport Family Foundation dissertation grant: a survey experiment among 1,800 White, Black, and Latino adults, and a conjoint among 900 Latino adults. Work of this kind provides many opportunities for undergraduate students to experience the research process, from designing surveys to cleaning data to analyzing and interpreting results.




Public Support and the Survival of High Courts


With Brandon Bartels and Eric Kramon · Two papers under revision


A Bayesian dynamic latent trait model pooling survey data across time and space to estimate public support for high courts in 145 countries since 1981. The measure itself is under revision at Political Science Research and Methods; the substantive finding, that elite attacks raise the likelihood of court-curbing and that public support significantly attenuates that link, is under revision at Comparative Political Studies.
